title: The Radon Nikodym Theorem and Lebesgue Decomposition

items.title: A positive, signed, or complex measure concentrated on a measurable set
Absolute continuity of a signed or complex measure with respect to a positive measure
A signed or complex measure that is both absolutely continuous and singular with respect to the same positive measure is zero
items.strategy: Use the singularity set on which the measure is concentrated. That set is null for the positive measure, so absolute continuity forces the measure to vanish on every measurable subset of it, and concentration then gives zero on every measurable set.

items.title: For signed and complex measures, absolute continuity is equivalent for the measure, its Jordan or real-imaginary parts, and its total variation
items.strategy: For signed measures use the Jordan formulas and test null sets termwise. For complex measures pass to the real and imaginary parts and compare their density formulas with total variation.

items.title: Every sigma-finite signed measure admits a Lebesgue decomposition relative to a sigma-finite positive measure
items.strategy: Reduce first to finite positive measures by sigma-finite exhaustion and Jordan decomposition. Among the nonnegative measurable g with int_A g dmu <= nu(A) for every measurable A, choose one with maximal integral by taking increasing maxima and monotone convergence; the residual measure is then singular by a Hahn-decomposition contradiction.

items.title: The Lebesgue decomposition of a sigma-finite signed measure is unique
items.strategy: Subtract two candidate decompositions. The difference of the absolutely continuous parts is also the difference of the singular parts, so it is simultaneously absolutely continuous and singular; the zero theorem forces equality.

items.title: The absolutely continuous part and the singular part in the Lebesgue decomposition
A sigma-finite signed measure that is absolutely continuous with respect to a sigma-finite positive measure has a unique almost-everywhere density
items.strategy: Apply the Lebesgue decomposition theorem to the signed measure. Absolute continuity forces the singular part to vanish, leaving only an indefinite integral against a measurable density; uniqueness follows because equal indefinite integrals imply equality almost everywhere.

items.title: A finite complex measure absolutely continuous with respect to a sigma-finite positive measure has an integrable complex density
items.strategy: Apply the signed Radon-Nikodym theorem to the real and imaginary parts and combine the resulting real densities into one complex L^1 density.

items.title: The Radon-Nikodym derivative as an almost-everywhere equivalence class
Integrating against a Radon-Nikodym derivative recovers integration against the measure
items.strategy: Prove the identity first for indicators and simple functions from the definition of the density. Extend to nonnegative measurable functions by monotone convergence and to L^1(nu) functions by linearity and simple-function density.

items.title: Radon-Nikodym derivatives add almost everywhere
items.strategy: The sum of the two candidate densities has the same measurable-set integrals as the derivative of the sum measure, so uniqueness of Radon-Nikodym derivatives gives equality almost everywhere.

items.title: Radon-Nikodym derivatives satisfy the chain rule along nu << mu << lambda
items.strategy: Integrate the product of the two intermediate densities over a measurable set and compare that value with nu of the same set. Uniqueness of the lambda-density then forces the almost-everywhere identity.

items.title: Equivalent sigma-finite positive measures have reciprocal Radon-Nikodym derivatives almost everywhere
items.strategy: Apply the chain rule to the identity measure viewed through the two mutually absolutely continuous measures and use that the self-derivative is 1 almost everywhere.

items.title: The total variation of an absolutely continuous signed or complex measure has density the absolute value of the Radon-Nikodym derivative
items.strategy: For signed measures use the Jordan formulas for a density. For complex measures apply the complex-density total-variation theorem to the Radon-Nikodym density obtained from the complex measure.

items.title: The Radon-Nikodym derivative is integrable exactly when the absolutely continuous part is finite
items.strategy: The integral of the absolute value of the density is the total variation of the absolutely continuous part. Thus L^1 integrability is equivalent to finiteness of that part.

items.title: For finite signed or complex measures, absolute continuity is equivalent to the epsilon-delta small-set condition
items.strategy: If nu = h dmu, use the absolute continuity of the integral for |h|. Conversely apply the scalar criterion to the total variation measure and then transfer back to nu through the absolute-continuity equivalence theorem.

items.title: Every finite signed or complex measure has a polar decomposition against its total variation
items.strategy: Because every finite signed or complex measure is absolutely continuous with respect to its total variation, Radon-Nikodym gives a density h against |nu|. The absolute-value formula forces |h| = 1 almost everywhere; in the signed case h takes the values plus or minus 1 and recovers the Hahn-Jordan pieces.

items.title: Every finite Borel measure on R has a unique absolutely continuous, discrete, and singular-continuous decomposition
items.strategy: Split first into atomic and atomless parts by the published Borel-measure theorem. Apply the Lebesgue decomposition to the atomless part relative to Lebesgue measure; the singular atomless remainder is the singular-continuous part, and uniqueness follows from the uniqueness of both preceding decompositions.

items.title: Von Neumann's Hilbert-space proof of Radon-Nikodym is shorter but depends on L^2 Riesz representation

title: The Radon Nikodym Theorem and Lebesgue Decomposition — Examples

items.title: The density $2x$ on $[0,1]$ is the Radon-Nikodym derivative of its density measure
items.strategy: Define the measure by its explicit density and use uniqueness of the Radon-Nikodym derivative.

items.title: The Lebesgue decomposition of one half Lebesgue plus one half Cantor measure
items.strategy: Lebesgue measure and Cantor measure are already mutually singular, so the decomposition is visible term by term.

items.title: The measure $\delta_0+\lambda\!\restriction_{[0,1]}$ splits into discrete and absolutely continuous parts
items.strategy: The point mass is atomic and singular, while the restricted Lebesgue measure has density 1 on [0,1].

items.title: The chain rule for Radon-Nikodym derivatives on $[0,1]$
items.strategy: Take dmu = 2 dlambda on [0,1] and dnu = 6x dlambda on [0,1], compute dnu/dmu and dmu/dlambda, and multiply them.

items.title: A piecewise-quadratic distribution function recovers its density
items.strategy: Check that the half-open interval increments of the distribution function agree with the integral of 2x 1_[0,1], then invoke uniqueness of the associated Lebesgue-Stieltjes measure.

items.title: Counting measure on $[0,1]$ shows the dominating measure needs sigma-finiteness
items.strategy: Counting measure on [0,1] is not sigma-finite. If Lebesgue measure were f dc for some density f, then for each x in [0,1] we would have 0 = lambda({x}) = int_{ {x} } f dc = f(x), because the singleton restriction is a one-atom simple function and counting measure gives {x} mass 1. Hence f = 0 everywhere, contradicting lambda([0,1]) = 1.

items.title: $x^{-1}d\lambda$ on $(0,1)$ shows finiteness is needed in the epsilon-delta criterion
items.strategy: The density x^{-1} is measurable, so the measure is absolutely continuous. But every interval (0,delta/2) has Lebesgue measure less than delta and infinite x^{-1} mass.

items.title: Two Radon-Nikodym derivatives can differ on a null set
items.strategy: Change an explicit density on a Lebesgue-null singleton. Every measurable-set integral stays unchanged, but the pointwise functions differ.

items.title: Lebesgue plus counting measure has no Lebesgue decomposition relative to Lebesgue measure
items.strategy: The Lebesgue summand forces a nonzero absolutely continuous part, while the counting summand cannot be concentrated on any Lebesgue-null set. Thus the sum cannot equal an absolutely continuous measure plus a singular measure.

items.title: An absolutely continuous finite measure can have an unbounded Radon-Nikodym derivative
items.strategy: Take dnu = x^(-1/2) 1_(0,1] dlambda. The total mass is finite but the density is unbounded near 0.

items.title: FALSE: every measure is absolutely continuous or singular with respect to Lebesgue measure
items.strategy: Refute with Lebesgue measure plus counting measure on [0,1], which has both an absolutely continuous summand and a genuinely nonsingular atomic summand.

items.title: FALSE: the Radon-Nikodym derivative is a uniquely determined function
items.strategy: Refute by changing a density on a null set. The resulting functions are different pointwise but define the same measure.

items.title: FALSE: the epsilon-delta condition characterises absolute continuity for every measure
items.strategy: Refute with x^{-1} 1_(0,1) dlambda, which is absolutely continuous and sigma-finite but violates the epsilon-delta conclusion.

items.title: FALSE: the Radon-Nikodym theorem holds without sigma-finiteness
items.strategy: Refute with Lebesgue measure relative to counting measure on [0,1], which is absolutely continuous but has no density against counting measure.

items.title: FALSE: absolutely continuous measures always have bounded Radon-Nikodym derivatives
items.strategy: Refute with the measure having density x^(-1/2) on (0,1], whose derivative exists and is unbounded.
